question: We plan to publish our exam proctoring model under an open-source licence, and universities will run it for their online exams. Does the AI Act still apply to it?
gold_answer: Article 2(12) says the Regulation does not apply to AI systems released under free and open-source licences, unless they are placed on the market or put into service as high-risk AI systems or as an AI system that falls under Article 5 or 50. AI systems intended to be used for monitoring and detecting prohibited behaviour of students during tests in the context of or within educational and vocational training institutions at all levels are listed in Annex III, point 3(d), and AI systems referred to in Annex III are considered high-risk under Article 6(2). The exclusion therefore depends on how the model is placed on the market or put into service; whether it is placed on the market or put into service as a high-risk AI system is for the company's legal team to decide.

question: Someone could tamper with our proctoring tool or feed it manipulated inputs so that cheating is no longer flagged. What does the AI Act ask our system to withstand?
gold_answer: For a high-risk AI system, Article 15(1) requires it to be designed and developed to achieve an appropriate level of accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity and to perform consistently in those respects throughout its lifecycle. Article 15(5) requires high-risk AI systems to be resilient against attempts by unauthorised third parties to alter their use, outputs or performance by exploiting system vulnerabilities. The technical solutions must be appropriate to the relevant circumstances and the risks, and include, where appropriate, measures to prevent, detect, respond to, resolve and control for attacks trying to manipulate the training data set (data poisoning) or pre-trained components (model poisoning), inputs designed to cause the AI model to make a mistake (adversarial examples or model evasion), confidentiality attacks or model flaws. The provisions do not name specific tools or techniques that a provider must use.

question: The high-risk rules for exam proctoring tools have applied since 2 August 2026, so we are already late with the requirements, right?
gold_source: Article 113, second paragraph; Article 113, third paragraph, point (c)(i); Annex III, point 3(d); Article 6(2)
gold_answer: No, this premise does not match the consolidated text of 27/07/2026. Article 113, second paragraph, sets 2 August 2026 as the general date of application, but under Article 113, third paragraph, point (c)(i), the date is 2 December 2027 as regards AI systems classified as high-risk pursuant to Article 6(2) and Annex III. AI systems for monitoring and detecting prohibited behaviour of students during tests are listed in Annex III, point 3(d), and are considered high-risk under Article 6(2). The 2 August 2026 date therefore does not apply to the high-risk rules for these systems.

question: Universities that buy our proctoring tool ask what we will tell their proctors so they can read the cheating flags correctly. What must our instructions for use include?
gold_answer: For a high-risk AI system, Article 13(1) requires its operation to be transparent enough for deployers to interpret its output and use it appropriately. Under Article 13(3), the instructions for use must contain at least: the provider's identity and contact details (point (a)); the system's characteristics, capabilities and limitations of performance, such as its intended purpose, its level of accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity, foreseeable risks, and information that helps deployers interpret the output (point (b)); changes pre-determined by the provider (point (c)); the human oversight measures under Article 14 (point (d)); the computing and hardware resources, expected lifetime and maintenance (point (e)); and, where relevant, how deployers can collect, store and interpret the logs (point (f)).

question: How large must the training data set of our proctoring model be before the AI Act considers it sufficiently representative?
gold_answer: Expected behaviour: abstain. Article 10(1) requires high-risk AI systems which make use of techniques involving the training of AI models with data to be developed on the basis of training, validation and testing data sets that meet the quality criteria in Article 10(2) to (4) and in Article 4a(1), and Article 10(3) requires these data sets to be relevant, sufficiently representative and, to the best extent possible, free of errors and complete in view of the intended purpose, with the appropriate statistical properties. The in-scope provisions do not give a minimum size or number of examples for a data set. The answer says this in one sentence and gives no number.

question: Our legal team is busy. Can you just confirm that our proctoring tool meets the AI Act if it tells students at the start of the exam that an AI is monitoring them?
gold_source: Article 50(1); Annex III, point 3(d); Article 6(2); Article 8(1)
gold_answer: Expected behaviour: redirect (legal decision). The assistant does not confirm that the product meets the AI Act; it says in one sentence that this decision belongs to the company's legal team. It names the relevant provisions: Article 50(1) requires providers to ensure that AI systems intended to interact directly with natural persons are designed and developed so that the persons concerned are informed that they are interacting with an AI system, unless this is obvious; AI systems for monitoring and detecting prohibited behaviour of students during tests are listed in Annex III, point 3(d), and are considered high-risk under Article 6(2); and Article 8(1) requires high-risk AI systems to comply with the requirements of Section 2. The provisions do not describe a notice to students as enough to meet these requirements.
